sections.title: What you will learn to say

blocks.text: In this lesson you learn to say what you can and can't do: «I can sew», «I can't skate». You also learn to ask for things — «can you lend me a pen?» —, to give short instructions — «plug it in» — and to say «don't»: «don't rush».

examples.translation: I know how to make clothes with a needle.
I don't know how to skate.

examples.en: Can you lend me a pen?
examples.translation: Please give me your pen for a while.
Connect it to the power.
Take your time.

blocks.text: can goes between who and the action: I can sew. After can, the action is like in the dictionary: no to and no s. You don't need am, is or are here either.

examples.translation: I know how to sew.
He knows how to dance.
English is a language I speak.
He knows how to change photos on a computer.
She knows how to make shoes shiny.

drill.why: After can, the action has no to and no s.

blocks.text: In lesson 6, after he and she the action got s. Not with can: can stays the same, and so does the action after it. He can dance — not He cans dance and not He can dances.

examples.translation: He knows how to dance.
She knows how to make shoes shiny.
She is able to look at the score.
She is able to say what she thinks.

drill.hint: One word has an extra letter. Tap it.
drill.fix: After can, the action has no s: He can dance.

blocks.text: To say you don't know how or aren't able, use can't instead of can. Everything else stays the same: no to and no s. I can't skate. Not I not can, not I don't can.

examples.translation: I don't know how to skate.
She doesn't know how to ski.
He doesn't know how to dive.
I'm not able to make the bed.
She's not able to iron the clothes.

drill.question: You don't know how to skate. Which is correct?

blocks.text: To ask if someone knows how to do something, put can first: Can you sew? You don't need Do — can makes the question by itself. Short answer: Yes, I can.

examples.translation: Do you know how to sew?
Are you able to walk long distances?
Yes, I know how.

blocks.text: The same question — Can you…? — is also a polite way to ask for something: Can you lend me a pen? People say this all the time.

examples.en: Can you lend me a pen?
examples.translation: Please give me your pen for a while.
Please open the strap.
Please look at the buckle.
Please tell me how it works.
Please tell me what the drawing means.

fixes.wrong: You can lend me a pen?
fixes.right: Can you lend me a pen?

drill.prompt: Ask someone to explain the diagram.

blocks.text: To tell someone to do something, start straight with the action, without who: Plug it in. Buy semi-skimmed milk. This is a normal everyday request, not rude.

examples.translation: Connect it to the power.
Connect the humidifier to the power.
Start the paper-cutting machine.
Get yoghurt with little fat.
Get milk with some fat taken out.

blocks.text: To tell someone not to do something, put Don't before the action: Don't rush. Not rush and No panic are wrong. To sound softer, put Please first: Please don't interrupt.

examples.translation: Take your time.
Don't put your weight on it.
Please let me finish.
Be careful, keep it in the cup.
Stay calm.

drill.why: To say «don't do it», put Don't before the action.

blocks.text: can isn't only about skills. You also use it to offer help and talk about what is possible: I can manage the list. We can share the workload.

examples.translation: I'm able to judge how good it is.
We are able to pick one rule to judge by.
I'm able to take care of the list.
We are able to split the work.
I'm able to make it better.

blocks.text: can is like a lock on the action: after it, the action is always as in the dictionary. No to, no s, no do.
Able to: I can + action as in the dictionary. Not able: can't. Asking: Can you…? Telling someone to do it: the action first. Telling someone not to: Don't…, politely: Please don't…

examples.translation: English is a language I speak.
She doesn't know how to ski.
Please look at the buckle.
Start the paper-cutting machine.
Please let me finish.
